stories.title: Traces of Justice review – ‘Chinese Sherlock Holmes’ at centre of arresting forensic cop thriller
stories.summary: Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases The latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise , offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi , a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional. Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. (Their scars are a terrific visual gag: scientists literally showing their working.) By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. Based on real scientist Cui Daozhi, this sharp feature has thumping set pieces and knotty puzzles set across 30 years of gripping cases

T he latest from Chen Sicheng, prime mover behind the hit Detective Chinatown franchise , offers a disarming mix of propaganda, copaganda and gripping narrative. It’s essentially a portmanteau biopic: its hero is Cui Xun, a fictional stand-in for the venerable Cui Daozhi , a still-extant real-life figure who so revolutionised forensic science he became known as “China’s Sherlock Holmes”. Ripping three-and-a-bit tales from the casebook – involving a 1970s child killer, a grisly 1980s multiple murder and a 1990s bus bombing (plus one lingering loose end), Chen constructs a history of forensic investigation that is also, in variably oblique ways, a history of Chinese law enforcement, which is shown evolving from boozy, gloveless crime-scene trampling to something far more streamlined and professional.

Within the handsome period framework, Chen follows the science: one era’s crazy innovation becomes commonplace in the next. A rookie Cui (played here by Zhang Yi, ageing up subtly) uses boiled potatoes to take dental imprints; when these run out, he and his colleagues start biting one another’s cheeks to make their points. (Their scars are a terrific visual gag: scientists literally showing their working.) By the 90s, when Cui is heading a team working out of a vast, well-staffed warehouse, we seem mere moments away from David Caruso’s sunglasses and memorable Who guitar riffs. The forbidding subtext is presumably that, after 50 years of such breakthroughs, there’s no more getting away with it; as one suspect insists: “everyone pays for what they’ve done.”

Yet Chen’s impressively limber storytelling also accommodates thumping set pieces and knotty forensic puzzle-solving. Remaining necessarily alert to key details, Zhang, in a likable unshowy turn, really does look like someone who’s spent long afternoons studying fingernail structure. The character’s personal life soon drifts out of focus, but the wider picture compels: a culture both becoming more baroque in its sociopathy – the bus bombers are an Asian equivalent to Leopold and Loeb – and sharpening its eye. (End titles also cite the centrality of Cui’s work to China’s current surveillance schemes.) Chen is pursuing reassuring closure and creates an arresting, effective feature besides.

stories.title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
stories.summary: Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Ukraine competes with Russia and data centers for China’s optical fiber supply.

Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones.

Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider .

Ukraine and Russia have been producing an estimated 50,000 fiber-optic drones per month in recent years. That’s a lot of optical fiber that has effectively become a one-time battlefield consumable.

But China’s economic and security ties with Russia have enabled Russia to import significantly larger amounts of fiber-optic cable than Ukraine—at least according to China’s official customs data. For example, Russia imported 328,000 miles of fiber-optic cable from China in August 2025 alone, compared to Ukraine getting just 72 miles of cable from Chinese companies, according to The Washington Post .

To get a better sense of how drone warfare has increased demand for optical fiber technology, Russia alone bought more than 37 million miles (60 million kilometers) of fiber-optic cable in 2025, according to The Insider and Russian business publication Vedomosti . That means Russia’s purchases amounted to more than 10 percent of all fiber produced worldwide last year, when it had previously never accounted for more than 1 percent of global demand.

The global AI boom and ongoing data center buildout have also strained optical fiber supply, with an expected worldwide shortfall of 111 million miles (180 million kilometers) in 2026, according to the market research firm TrendForce . That has further increased the cost of optical fiber purchased by Russia and Ukraine, including the bend-insensitive fiber that is especially coveted for fiber-optic drones.

One Ukrainian drone manufacturer navigating these supply chain challenges is BlueBird Tech, which produces fiber-optic drones along with other military drones, a ground robot, drone detection systems, and electronic warfare systems. Ars reached out to BlueBird Tech to learn more.

The following Q&A represents written responses from Oleksiy, a BlueBird Tech R&D representative, after an initial conversation with Ars. The responses have been lightly edited for clarity. Oleksiy is only being identified by first name for security reasons.

Ars Technica: How has the use of fiber-optic drones by Ukraine and Russia evolved, and where does the technology stand today?

Oleksiy: Fiber-optic drones are a specific type of drone used for particular operations. One of their main characteristics is that they do not produce the same radio-frequency (RF) emissions as conventional RF-controlled FPV drones. That means conventional RF detectors cannot detect them in the same way, and electronic warfare systems cannot disrupt their control link in the same way either.

At the same time, fiber-optic drones have their own operational limitations. A pilot who is experienced with a conventional RF-controlled FPV drone cannot necessarily switch immediately to a fiber-optic drone. It requires specific skills, and fiber-optic drones have different flight characteristics.

So there are significant advantages, particularly when operating in an electronic warfare environment, but there are also limitations in terms of operation, pilot training, and cost.

Because of the high density of electronic intelligence and electronic warfare systems on the battlefield, using conventional radio-controlled FPV drones has become increasingly difficult.

Fiber-optic technology provides a way to operate in these conditions, although it also comes with certain limitations.

So today, both sides are using fiber-optic drones on the battlefield, but radio-controlled drones still make up the larger share overall.

Ars Technica: What are the main disadvantages or limitations of fiber-optic drones?

Oleksiy: One of the biggest limitations today is cost. If we compare fiber-optic prices in 2025 and 2026, we have seen increases of roughly six to ten times. The most difficult period in terms of prices and shortages was around March. Since then, the situation has stabilized to some extent.

But the underlying issue remains that the material primarily comes from China. That means Ukrainian manufacturers depend on Chinese supply, logistics, availability, and pricing.

There is also broader global demand for fiber-optic material. FPV drones are only one application. Data centers around the world consume large amounts of fiber, and the growth of AI infrastructure is also contributing to demand.

So Ukrainian drone manufacturers are operating within a much larger global market for fiber optic, and that affects both availability and price.

Ars Technica: How are Ukrainian manufacturers adapting to these supply-chain and quality challenges?

Oleksiy: One important change is that many manufacturers are moving the spooling process in-house. Instead of buying a finished fiber-optic spool for an FPV drone, they can buy the fiber in much larger spools and produce the smaller drone spools themselves.

This does not remove the dependence on China for the material itself, but it gives manufacturers more control over the finished product.

Quality is a major reason for doing this. We have seen problems and defects in finished spools supplied from China. By doing the spooling themselves, manufacturers can introduce their own quality-control procedures and achieve a more consistent result.

It can also make the finished spool somewhat cheaper than buying a finished product in China and transporting it to Ukraine.

But quality is the most important factor. If a fiber-optic spool has a defect, you can lose the drone, lose the mission, and lose the target.

Fiber optic is also not the only component in this supply chain. Media converters are another component manufacturers need to source, and China is important for that supply as well.

Ars Technica: So Ukrainian companies are buying large quantities of fiber and producing the FPV spools domestically?

Oleksiy: Yes. A manufacturer can buy a large spool of fiber-optic material and then use that material to produce smaller spools designed for FPV drones.

That also allows the manufacturer to perform its own quality checks during production rather than relying entirely on the quality of a finished imported spool.

Ars Technica: Has this become the standard approach across the Ukrainian industry?

Oleksiy: It depends on the manufacturer and on the size of the company. Larger companies may have the resources to do the spooling themselves. That requires spooling equipment, people who understand the process, testing capabilities, and quality control.

Smaller manufacturers may not have those resources. In those cases, they may buy finished spools from larger Ukrainian manufacturers or from suppliers abroad, including China.

So there is no single model across the industry. It largely depends on the scale and capabilities of each manufacturer.

Ars Technica: Can Ukraine source fiber-optic material from countries other than China?

Oleksiy: You can buy fiber-optic material through suppliers in other countries, but in practice China remains the main source in this market.

There can be intermediaries in other countries, and prices can differ depending on the country and the purchasing route.

But in the end, China remains the main source of the fiber-optic material we are talking about.

Ars Technica: Have Ukrainian companies experienced actual shortages or situations where suppliers were unable or unwilling to fill orders?

Oleksiy: Yes, there have been situations like that. It depends on many factors, including how the material is purchased, which supplier is involved, and the logistics.

There have also been cases where Chinese manufacturers have told Ukrainian buyers that they did not have material available for them because they were from Ukraine.

Russia also has more direct logistics with China, so from a practical supply-chain perspective it has an easier route for sourcing this material.

Ars Technica: Are there other important supply-chain challenges beyond availability and price?

Oleksiy: Yes. Logistics is another important factor. Once the material reaches Ukraine, it still has to pass through customs and then be transported to manufacturers.

Air raid alerts can interrupt this process. Customs operations and other parts of the logistics chain may stop during alerts, which adds time before the material reaches the manufacturer. So companies have to take these delays into account when planning production.

There are also security considerations. I cannot discuss specific cases involving attacks on fiber-optic production because of security restrictions. But manufacturers are potential targets for the enemy, so security measures are extremely important for developers, suppliers, and manufacturers.

Ars Technica: Is the physical transportation route from China to Ukraine also a challenge?

Oleksiy: Yes. The route from China to Ukraine is much longer, and that creates challenges in terms of both time and logistics costs.

So the problem is not only obtaining the material itself. Manufacturers also have to account for the time and expense required to transport it over a long distance.

Ars Technica: How do these price, logistics, and supply-chain challenges affect how a drone manufacturer approaches fiber-optic systems?

Oleksiy: Planning becomes extremely important. You need to plan production and logistics together. If you understand your manufacturing requirements in advance, you can plan your logistics and your next orders accordingly.

Having more of the manufacturing process under your own control is also important.

Quality is another major factor. If the fiber has fewer defects, you can produce more usable FPV spools from one large spool of material. If there are many defects, you ultimately produce fewer usable spools from the same amount of fiber.

So production planning, logistics planning, in-house manufacturing capabilities, material quality, and the skills of the people doing the work are all closely connected.

Ars Technica: Does producing fiber-optic spools require specially trained personnel?

Oleksiy: Yes. We do not have universities that specifically train people to manufacture these FPV fiber-optic spools. So it comes down to training, training, and more training.

When people first learn the process, they naturally make mistakes and create defects. They need practical experience to improve.

Training itself also consumes fiber-optic material because people have to practice the actual manufacturing process.

So developing skilled personnel is another part of scaling production. The goal is to develop the skills required to manufacture consistently high-quality spools with as few defects as possible.

Ars Technica: What makes manufacturing a fiber-optic spool technically difficult?

Oleksiy: You need to understand a lot about the fiber itself, about the spooling process, and about what happens when the fiber unwinds from the spool during operation.

Fiber-optic cable is fragile and can be damaged or broken relatively easily. If something goes wrong during manufacturing or while the fiber is unwinding, you can damage the fiber and lose the connection.

That is why practical experience is so important. You need to practice the manufacturing process, and that can require many kilometers of fiber just for training.

The equipment used for spooling also matters. If you use low-quality equipment or the equipment is not configured properly, you can introduce more defects into the finished spool.

So both the equipment and the people operating it affect the quality of the final product.

Ars Technica: How automated is the spooling process?

Oleksiy: It depends on the type of equipment. Some systems require more manual involvement, while others are more automated.

But even with automated equipment, skilled personnel are still required. Someone has to configure the equipment correctly and understand how the process works. The way the system is set up also affects the quality of the finished product.

So automation does not remove the need for expertise.

Ars Technica: How do manufacturers test the quality of finished fiber-optic spools?

Oleksiy: There are different levels of testing. Every finished spool should be checked to make sure the optical link itself is working properly.

But if you want to ensure consistent production quality, that is not enough. You also need to take a portion of the finished spools from a production batch, install them on actual FPV drones, and fly them under real conditions.

That allows you to test not only the optical connection itself, but also whether the finished spool performs properly during an actual flight.

So every spool should undergo link testing, while some of the finished spools from each production batch should also be tested in real flights. That combination is important if you want to maintain consistent quality in production.

stories.title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
stories.summary: Huang, who is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, is far more important to the future of the world order than other tech bosses.

Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025

Published 10 November 2026, 06:01 GMT

Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.

Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.

Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy .

Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.

Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.

I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.

It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."

He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.

Differing views on security risks

However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.

Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.

The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.

Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".

He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".

What does this show us?

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.

More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.

Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.

Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

Introduction: Nvidia hit by shareholder lawsuit

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

The fallout over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy is intensifying, after the AI chipmaking firm has been hit with a shareholder lawsuit.

According to a complaint filed in federal court in San Jose, ​California, the defendants misled shareholders about Huang’s alleged ​affair with Alice Huang , a former executive of Singapore-based ⁠ Megaspeed , and did ​not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that ​threatened Nvidia’s reputation and business prospects.

The suit also claims that Huang’s failure to disclose the affair artificially inflated Nvidia’s share price, and could have violated federal securities laws, Politico reported.

Nvidia’s share price took a knock yesterday – falling by 3.2% and cutting the company’s valuation by almost $200bn, to $4.3tn.

Huang’s reputation has taken a serious knock, after he admitted being unfaithful to his wife following reports of an affair with Nvidia customer and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang .

As Megaspeed has been accused of illicitly smuggling and diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China, the ramifications are serious.

Donald Trump weighed in over the scandal yesterday, telling reporters:

double quotation mark “I asked him [Mr Huang] about that and he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

Trump also told a news conference that the US Federal Bureau of Investigation was involved in the case, saying:

double quotation mark “We’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else.”

The agenda

8am GMT: Worldpanel UK supermarket inflation data

From 9am GMT: Bank of England Watchers’ Conference in London

11am GMT: NFIB index of US business optimism

1.30pm GMT: US inflation report for October

Cunliffe: A correction is coming....

Q: Is the world heading toward a financial crisis, and can we get out of it?

Sir Jon Cunliffe (who was a senior member of HM Treasury during the 2008 crisis), tells the Bank of England and its Watchers conference that a market correction is coming.

He says:

double quotation mark To me it’s pretty clear that a correction will happen. The issue isn’t whether it’s coming, it’s whether it transmits though the financial system.

Cunliffe – a former Bank of England deputy governor – explains that policymakers normally worry when they see leverage involved in a boom.

Cunliffe’s “two poles” are the dotcom bust of 2000 – which inflicted losses on asset holders without creating a financial crisis – and the sub-prime crisis of 2008, which did ripple out into a financial crisis.

The difference between those two events is the interconnection and leverage. And it looks more and more that there is interconnection and leverage this time, Cunliffe cautions.

A mrket crash could lead to a credit crunch where everyone sells everything they can, Cunliffe continues. And if that happens, the tools a central bank would use look like the tools you’d use for other crises, he adds.

Nvidia faces a “difficult road ahead”, warns Niall Hearty, partner and regulatory lawyer at legal firm Weightmans:

double quotation mark “Shareholder lawsuits and an independent internal investigation will mean a difficult road ahead for the world’s second-largest company, particularly as Nvidia faces wider pressure from investors amid growing concerns around AI investment and the future of the sector. There are also wider questions to be asked about national security and the protection of commercially sensitive information at a time when the US and China are racing to gain technological supremacy.”

Q: The Americans showed valuable leadership after the 2008 crisis – do you have confidence that if there is another major crisis the US would exercise leadership again? And would they be followed?

Professor Sir David Osmand tells the Bank of England and its Watchers conference there are two kinds of crisis.

“If the financial windows have been blown in,” he expects the US to step up, as it would be in their interest.

He’s more worried about a “slowburn crisis” – such as unregulated tokenisation.

There, the interests of the US may diverge from other countries, such as those in Europe, Osmand explains.

Spencer Dale , professor of practice at the London School of Economics , says the development of AI is likely to be the most significant source of risk.

The world has “completely failed” to agree any global response to AI, or agree a regulatory response, he says.

Instead, at points of stress - such as the risks from the Mythos AI model – the US has moved the other way, keeping information to itself.

Dale explains:

double quotation mark “Thus far I am not hugely comforted by the way the world has responded to the need to think about and talk about, and then sensibly regulate, AI at a global level.”

George Osborne: UK has opportunity to lead crypto world

Over at the Digital Asset Summit in London, the former chancellor George Osborne is wearing one of his many hats as adviser to the crypto exchange Coinbase .

Osborne, who also recently joined the ChatGPT developer OpenAI , has suggested that the UK has the opportunity to be a leader in crypto innovation after the US mid-term elections, my colleague Lauren Almeida reports.

He said:

double quotation mark “The UK often has opportunity historically when the US system… can be more bureaucratic and fails to take advantage of a financial innovation.”

His comments come as the crypto industry frets over a less friendly environment in the US, where president Donald Trump’s control has been weakened by the midterm election result. His government had taken “pretty decisive steps forward on crypto regulation”, Osborne said.

Trump himself has been particularly bullish on the sector, having vowed to make the US the “crypto capital of the world” and pushed for deregulation of the industry. Last year he pardoned Changpeng Zhao — founder of the recently hacked crypto exchange Binance — who had been jailed after pleading guilty to failing to protect against money laundering.

That is not to mention Trump’s personal wealth in the sector — he made at least $1.4bn from his crypto ventures last year, according to financial disclosures he made in June.

But Osborne added that it was “too soon to know exactly what is going to happen” with the US approach to the sector.

double quotation mark “It is a bit simplistic to say Democrats are anti innovation in finance and Republicans are pro innovation in finance. There are [Democrats] who have led the case for innovation in the space.”

Why fiscal pressures are rising

Central banks will face rising political pressure to keep interest rates low, potentially moving us towards an era of fiscal dominance, the Bank of England Watchers conference is hearing.

Professor Beata Javorcik, chief economist at EBRD and professor of economics at Oxford, cites three reasons why pressure will rise:

Rising fiscal burden . “It’s no secret that governments have been borrowing like there is no tomorrow,” she points out, citing pressures such as the Covid pandemic, and the energy shock. That has created an expectation that politiciant will step in when there’s a crisis.

Growing public demand for a larger state

Demographics , and the challenge of an aging populations. Pensions are a “very toxic topic” when it comes to the amount spent on pensions, Javorcik points out – citing opposition in France to pension cuts. She points out that the median person in advanced economies in 1950 was 29. Now the median person is 41. As electorates gets older, support for spending more on pensions will rise, she adds.

[Those three pressures mean governments will not want higher interest rates, as that pushes up their cost of borrowing].

AI could create Liz Truss-like crisis 'at warp speed'

Over at IET Savoy Place, on the north bank of the Thames, the Bank of England Watchers conference organised by King’s Business School is underway.

Professor Sir David Osmand , of King’s College London, is talking about the threats posed by agentic AI.

Osmand explains that frontier AI is already given elite hacking capability to unskilled actors, putting those tools within the reach of anyone with “an API key and a digital wallet”

He then cites the push towards widespread tokanisation within finance – putting real world assets on the blockchain.

And that move will create opportunities for AI to attack everything around that digital ledger.

Harking back to the crisis after the 2022 mini-budget, when UK government bond prices crashed before the Bank of England stepped in , Osmand says:

double quotation mark In a sense, we’ve seen this film before. Liz Truss 2022, with the LDI episode, and collateral calls from gilts forcing the bank to intervene. That happened at human speed and excellent work by the bank that produced the next day settlement. But just imagine when that happens with a frontier AI-driven crisis at warp speed.

The reference to Liz Truss gives former Bank governor Sir Jon Cunliffe a nasty flashback. “I still have PTSD about that,” he jokes.

Bonuses for Wall Street’s investment bankers are forecast to jump more than 30% this year, but bankers have been warned to enjoy the party while it lasts.

Analysts at financial services compensation consultancy Johnson Associates estimate that investment bankers, particularly stock traders and underwriters, are due to see a 20% to 30%+ jump in the size of bonuses compared to 2025.

It will mark the third straight year of ballooning bonuses for Wall Street bankers, after a trading boom led by tech firms and AI-linked stocks. (which have of course suffered a post-US-midterm election correction).

Alan Johnson , managing director of Johnson Associates said:

“Although bank stocks have been softer this year, record results in equity trading and underwriting have made 2026 the ‘year of the bank,’ and those professionals are in line to receive the largest increases.

“Given the industry’s overall performance, we project that most professionals will see higher incentives at year-end.”

However, the consultancy warned that 2026 will mark peak growth for banker bonuses, with geopolitical turmoil, rising inflation, and frothy stock prices due to hit company fundraising plans next year. Johnson said:

double quotation mark “We expect 2026 to mark a peak against a potentially weaker 2027. Geopolitical turmoil, rising inflation and elevated equity valuations add uncertainty to public markets while fundraising challenges and higher interest rates continue to weigh on private markets. “Against this backdrop, compensation strategies are likely to become increasingly differentiated, with greater dispersion based on firm and individual performance. “Talent sourcing and retention, disciplined structures and alignment with broader business priorities will remain key focal points.”

News website The Information are reporting that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing facilitated the shipment of at least $7.5bn worth of the company’s chips.

UK and Irish retail investors are continuing to invest in Nvidia despite uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang , according to trading platform IG.

IG reports that the number of clients buying shares in Nvidia surging 432% yesterday, compared with the average across the previous ten trading days.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, says there appears to be a broad wave of investor confidence, adding:

double quotation mark “But this is no ordinary dip-buying opportunity. Nvidia has become the poster child of the AI boom, and Huang has been central to its extraordinary rise. Any threat to his leadership risks shaking confidence not just in Nvidia, but in the wider technology rally.”

Bloomberg: Top UK regulator says banks are trimming AI risk

UK banks have begun cutting their exposure to artificial intelligence as alarm mounts that the sector could suffer a brutal correction, according to the Bank of England’s top supervisor.

Katharine Braddick told Bloomberg that the bank wasn’t being complacent, saying:

double quotation mark “We’re all alarmed at the moment, aren’t we?”

Banks are “all asking themselves that question” of whether to reduce exposure, Braddick added, explaining:

double quotation mark “I can see firms looking at their risk appetite and thinking and considering, ‘Yes this client, not that client.’ You do see it feed through.”

Nvidia shares up nearly 2% in premarket trading

Nvidia’s shares are set to rally when Wall Street opens in almost five hours time.

The company’s stock is up 1.8% in premarket trading, which would recover over a third of yesterday’s drop.

Dr Ammar Ahmed from the University of St Andrews Business School says it’s too early to assess impact of the scandal on Nvidia’s long-term valuation.

double quotation mark “When you have multiple confounding events, it is difficult to isolate a specific one as opposed to another as having an effect on the stock market. The current situation over the last week is a perfect storm to push down the value of AI stock. Potentially Nvidia may have compromised US national security as well as their own competitive edge. We don’t know if or what the woman, with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, has passed to the Chinese state. Secondly there is the political and legislative risk that comes from that. If Nvidia have failed on their part to protect US security around AI, the federal government could step in and regulate or impose some additional oversight that constrains not only Nvidia’s activities but potentially the entire sector in the future. It is enough to move the market as the reaction is around pricing as much as it is around valuation. With pricing, short-term traders in financial markets can take advantage of swings in share prices and make money from this shift in short-term expectations. But how these events affect the long-term valuation of a company is too early to see. It’s a wait and see game, particularly around what the democrats do. Until you see the outcome of those things still in play, it’s difficult to get a clearer picture of the long-term prospects for AI companies. “Already there’s been a rebound in tech share prices today, which is a sign that some investors may believe the recent events represent an overcorrection. But a one-day bounce reflects market sentiment rather than a reassessment of long-term value, and until the outstanding questions are resolved, prices are likely to remain volatile.”

Vodafone cuts 3,000 jobs in cost saving drive

Vodafone has cut 3,000 jobs across its European operation, as the telecoms company looks to make €2bn in cost savings by the end of the decade.

The UK-headquartered company said that the roles had been cut between April and September, helping to deliver €200m in cost savings.

This included €50m from its UK operation where the company continues to focus on synergies after it bought out the 49% stake it did not already own in VodafoneThree .

The company has said it expects to deliver £1bn in annual savings at VodafoneThree, the UK’s largest mobile operator, by 2032.

On Monday, the company announced a separate round of 2,300 job cuts in Germany, Vodafone’s biggest market, over the next two years.

On Tuesday, the company raised its profit and cash flow guidance for the current financial year, after reporting that group-wide revenues increased 11.4% year-on-year in its first half. In the UK, revenue increased 10% to €4.9bn.

The company said it now expects earnings before tax to come in at €13.2bn to €13.4bn for the year, following a previous range of €13bn to €13.3bn. The cash flow estimate was upgraded from €2.8bn to €3bn.

Vodafone reported 6.4% growth in adjusted earnings to €6.45bn for the first half.

Overall, the company reported a €3.6bn loss in the first half, after booking an almost €5bn impairment charge in Germany.

“I am very happy about our overall group performance, but Germany is not yet where it needs to be,” said Margherita Della Valle , Vodafone’s CEO.

Vodafone’s share price dipped slightly on Tuesday, but is up almost 30% over the last year.

Reuters: Huang's woes evoke sympathy and disbelief in his birthplace Taiwan

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is drawing both sympathy and disbelief in his birthplace Taiwan, where he ⁠has rock star status.

Reuters reports that the ⁠dramatic revelations of his ​affair with a woman who could have been a Chinese spy have not dented Huang’s popularity.

double quotation mark Shock at news that both Nvidia’s board and the FBI are investigating to determine if Huang was targeted by a ⁠foreign intelligence effort is palpable in the small Taipei businesses and restaurants he frequents on trips. “I thought it must be ​a lie, or fake news,” said Hsiao Kui-yu, whose ‌store selling dried and candied fruit ‌is among Huang’s inevitable stops at Taipei’s Siping market. “We think of him as such a good boss, who ‌takes such good care of people. How could something like this happen? Is it possible? I’m very suspicious,” Hsiao, 68, told Reuters. Huang’s barber Ray Wang, whose high-end shop is just around the corner from the luxury hotel where Huang often stays, said the two formed a bond when the CEO first visited in 2017. “Every day I pray for Mr. Huang, hoping he gets through this difficult time,” the 57-year-old added. “I really want to ‌write him a letter of encouragement, but I feel this isn’t a good time, because he’s very busy.”

Britons stockpiling water and food tins but not panic buying

British shoppers have been stocking up on essentials such as bottled water, tinned goods and hand sanitiser, but did not panic buy after the government advised people to prepare for emergencies, shopping data has shown.

Sales of essentials jumped in the 10 days after the government launched its Be Ready campaign , which encourages households to prepare for up to three days in the event of disruption to essential services from incidents such as cyber-attacks or extreme weather.

In the 10 days after the campaign launch, sales of hand sanitiser surged by 83% compared with the same period last year, while sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods went up 37%, according to Worldpanel by Numerator’s monthly grocery report for Great Britain.

The number of people buying tinned meat each day after the launch of the campaign rose by 43%, equivalent to an extra 400,000 shoppers a day, but the typical amount bought remained at about 500g in terms of pack size.

stories.body:
Published 53 minutes ago

Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.

Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.

The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.

Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.

Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".

The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".

stories.title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
stories.summary: Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Lawsuit demands Kalshi return losses because online betting is illegal in Washington.

A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington’s ban on online gambling. He’s trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000.

Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright’s “wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that,” said the gambler’s lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright’s case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits.

“Washington has prohibited Internet gambling since 2006. Washington has also provided, since long before that, a statutory cause of action permitting any person who loses money at illegal gambling to recover it from the proprietor for whose benefit the game was conducted,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

Even if Bright’s lawsuit fails, gamblers who lost on Kalshi could get money back through the lawsuits filed by state governments. For example, Washington’s lawsuit against the company said the attorney general “is entitled to recover all money Washingtonians have lost through Defendant Kalshi’s illegal gambling operation” under the state’s Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act. Washington already won a court order restricting the kinds of wagers Kalshi can offer in the state, but it took effect after Bright’s losses.

Kalshi says event contracts aren’t gambling

Kalshi wants Bright’s lawsuit to be moved to US District Court for the Western District of Washington, saying it must be tried in a federal court instead of a state one. In an October 30 motion to dismiss Bright’s case, Kalshi argued that he did not lose any money on “gambling.” Kalshi said he lost money on “event contracts,” which Kalshi says can only be regulated by the federal government.

“The contracts which Plaintiff mischaracterizes as gambling are event contracts offered on the Platform subject to the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act], in conformance with the rules and regulations of the CFTC [Commodity Futures Trading Commission], the federal agency which has statutory authority to oversee the CEA,” Kalshi said.

We contacted Bright’s attorney, Michael Daudt, about Kalshi’s court filings and will update this article if we get a response.

“Plaintiff alleges that his activity on the platform was gambling and that he ‘lost,’” Kalshi wrote. “He does not allege that anyone misled him about how the platform worked, what it charged, or the risk that any position might lose. Yet, he now sues KalshiEX and its parent, Kalshi Inc., to recover nearly double his own alleged net realized loss under Washington’s gambling loss-recovery statute, and a theory of unjust enrichment.”

Between June 17 and August 14, 2026, Bright transferred $315,353.94 to Kalshi in 253 separate debits from his checking account, his lawsuit said. Kalshi allegedly collected $5,589.05 in funding fees on those transfers.

Bright made numerous wagers on sporting events including professional baseball games and tennis matches. He apparently put any winnings into new bets, and alleges that “Kalshi’s platform cycled Plaintiff’s deposits through $14,396,457.30 in transactions and assessed and retained $84,062.71 in trading fees on them, equal to 26.7 percent of everything Plaintiff deposited.”

After all his bets, Bright suffered a net loss of $308,781.62, and his account was left with a balance of $983.27. Kalshi said that Bright’s “alleged losses went to counterparties rather than” to Kalshi itself and that Bright’s “positions were matched with counterparties and resolved according to the outcomes of the underlying events.”

“The Complaint does not allege that KalshiEX or Kalshi Inc. was the counterparty to any of Plaintiff’s positions,” Kalshi said.

Kalshi calls itself “a neutral exchange platform” with no financial stake in the outcome of any event. It makes revenue by collecting fees on transactions. But while Kalshi describes itself as a neutral operator and collector of transaction fees, its business model also includes a trading affiliate that places wagers on the platform.

Kalshi’s trading affiliate

Kalshi’s rulebook says its trading affiliate “participates on the Platform and provides liquidity to the Platform by placing orders on either (or both) sides of a market at competitive price levels.” Kalshi says its affiliate only has access to the same public information that other traders on the platform have.

Bright’s lawsuit alleges that Kalshi’s affiliate “took the opposite side of a substantial portion of Plaintiff’s positions,” meaning that “Kalshi and the enterprise under common ownership with it were not a neutral venue but the dealer or player winning within the meaning of [state law], in addition to being the proprietor for whose benefit the wagering was conducted.”

Bright doesn’t know for sure whether Kalshi’s affiliate was on the other side of any of his bets. “The identity of the participant on the opposite side of each of Plaintiff’s positions, and the profit each such participant realized, is information exclusively within Kalshi’s possession,” Bright’s lawsuit said.

The US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in August that Nevada can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws. Although that case involved Nevada, the Ninth Circuit’s jurisdiction includes the state of Washington. Bright’s lawsuit quoted the ruling’s finding that “placing sports bets, even when called by another name, is still gambling.”

Although Bright’s lawsuit said his net loss was $308,781.62, he asked for $580,544.98 based on an “event-by-event” calculation derived from a 1950 ruling issued by the Washington Supreme Court. “Computed on the event-by-event basis required by Heitfeld , under which winnings in separate and distinct events may not be offset against losses, the sums Plaintiff lost total $580,544.98,” the lawsuit said.

Bright’s lawsuit said that if the court declines to order $580,544.98 in restitution, it should instead award “all funds Plaintiff transferred to Kalshi and the $89,651.76 in funding and trading fees Kalshi collected.” That would amount to over $405,000.

Kalshi seeks delay until Supreme Court weighs in

In addition to its motion to dismiss the case, Kalshi filed a motion to stay the proceedings at least until the US Supreme Court decides whether to take up a separate case on whether state gambling laws apply to prediction markets. “The orderly course of justice favors a stay because Supreme Court review will settle or simplify every claim and ensure uniform treatment of like suits,” Kalshi told the US district court.

Kalshi has suffered some notable losses in US appeals courts, which found that states can regulate the platform’s event contracts under gambling laws. But federal courts have not unanimously sided with states, and New Jersey asked the Supreme Court to settle the question of whether states can regulate Kalshi under gambling laws.

Kalshi’s motion for a stay in the Bright case noted that Washington government officials are “pursuing overlapping claims” against Kalshi. “The State of Washington is pursuing the same theory, and seeks the same recovery for Mr. Bright, in a case pending before the Superior Court of Washington for King County,” Kalshi wrote.

Kalshi tried to get the state’s case moved to a federal court, but it was sent back to King County Superior Court in May. Washington won a preliminary injunction against Kalshi in August, when a King County judge ordered Kalshi to implement geofencing and stop allowing many types of wagers in the state.

The county court’s order required Kalshi to stop offering or accepting event contracts “related to sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions” in the state. The injunction did not affect wagers in the commodities, climate, economics, and finance categories.

Bright transferred his funds to Kalshi before the geofencing order took effect. His lawsuit claims that on September 15, he tried to access the app but received a notice that “using this app in your current location is prohibited.”

This article was updated to correct the date the lawsuit was filed .

stories.title: We’re Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches
stories.summary: Today , along with the ACLU, EFF filed an amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit court of appeals in United States v. Sturdivant , a case where police warrantlessly tracked a suspect’s movements using Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) data. Our brief details the vast, interconnected network of ALPRs that constantly track drivers around the country and argues that this tracking is a “search” under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment. Sturdivant involves a series of robberies in and around Cleveland, Ohio. Using surveillance camera footage, police identified the make, model, and color of the robber’s car, but they did not know its license plate number. After running an open-ended search of two ALPR databases, Flock and ELSAG, officers learned a car belonging to the defendant had been tracked near sites of the robberies, eventually leading to his arrest. Faced with a motion to suppress the ALPR evidence, the district court held that Mr. Sturdivant had no reasonable expectation of privacy in his license plate number because it could be observed by members of the public, and that therefore he had no Fourth Amendment interest in not having his car tracked in public places. But ALPRs are simply not comparable to observing an individual license plate on a passing car. As we’ve explained in many amicus briefs and in our lawsuits directly challenging ALPR use in San Jose, California and Wisconsin , ALPRs give law enforcement “ a virtual time machine to view suspects’, or anyone else’s, past movements (and much more) with just the click of a button.” Just last month, a federal district court agreed and held that ALPRs are a “ form of indiscriminate mass surveillance” that can violate the Fourth Amendment. We hope the Sixth Circuit will reverse the lower court in this case and hold that ALPR searches require a warrant. Related Cases: Wisconsin Council of Churches v. Milwaukee, Racine, Kenosha & Green Bay SIREN and CAIR-CA v. San Jose

stories.body:
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’

Cop31 live – latest updates

China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. “They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”

China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.

Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”

China as a ‘doer and go-getter’

The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .

Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.

The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue. “Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”

after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .

Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.

The need for trust

China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.

Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”

If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.

Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.

They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.

For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … So no major drama.”

stories.summary: The government says it is strengthening its guidance for schools in England, which came into force in June.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 9 November 2026

Pupils will not be allowed access to their phones at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.

Statutory guidance came into force in June, making schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.

Ministers now say changes to that guidance will go beyond the current "no see, no hear" policies in place in some schools - where phones can remain in pupils' bags if they are not seen or heard - when it comes into force from September 2027.

But head teachers' unions said schools would struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding from government.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government's "clear message" to parents and pupils was that "school is for learning and friendship, not scrolling".

Access to phones "risks pulling children away from their learning and from each other", the government said.

Schools will be able to decide how to follow the guidance. Some schools have invested in sealed pouches or secure lockers. Others collect phones at the start of the day, or have prohibited them from sites altogether.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Powell said such policies could achieve a "whole-school culture change" - and that was "what we want to see happening everywhere".

Karl Harrison, head teacher at Burnage Academy for Boys in Manchester, told the programme the school had spent £20,000 to bring in a system of metal detectors and phone pouches to prevent pupils from accessing their phones.

While some felt their freedom had gone, locking phones away had increased how much pupils socialised at school, he said.

"People now can talk to each other, instead of scrolling on a device," he said.

"It's also increased levels of focus in lessons because now there's less distraction, and people are achieving higher grades."

Some schools - like Brownhills Ormiston Academy, in the West Midlands - provide pupils with lockable pouches for their phones

Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear".

"If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said.

"This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."

Responding to questions about funding, Powell told BBC Breakfast that she wanted heads to have the autonomy to implement the policies that work best for their schools.

Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets".

"Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.

A smartphone ban in English schools is coming into force. What's changing? Published 27 June

Parents want to ban smartphones in schools, but there's one reason they're worried Published 31 January

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".

She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance .

But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.

Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.

In Scotland , external , the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.

In Wales , external , the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.

And in Northern Ireland , Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".

Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.

Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.

stories.title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
stories.summary: The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies. The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying. Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system. In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only 97 IPR petitions were filed at the PTAB, compared to 327 petitions during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only 37 IPR petitions were filed in September 2026, compared to 129 petitions in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges. This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology. That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong. Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard. It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. And then, instead of the familiar tiled battlefield, I was looking at a pixellated singer-songwriter, who launched into an extremely long preamble about the mating habits of the Pacific salmon before saying, “This is a song for anyone else who ever got so horny they could die,” and launching into a soulful acoustic guitar number accompanied by crude images of leaping fish.
